transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~62m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Leah (Cragmoor Head Infra), Arjun (Network), Samira (Security), Tom (PM)

Summary (auto): quick discovery on private onramp, went over peering options, egress patterns, and compliance asks.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we'll do quick intros then dive into your network constraints.
[00:12] Leah Park: Hi, Leah here. We're moving from a prototype hosted solution to something private—wanna understand what the network onramp looks like.
[00:18] Diego Alvarez: Cool, Diego from Redwood SE. We'll cover peering options, private endpoints, egress and KMS. Quick note: I'm going to draw a couple of topology sketches in the follow up.
[00:27] Tom: Quick note from product—latency SLOs are important for user-facing features, but security is hard requirement.
[00:33] Samira Noor: We're SOC2 in flight, and we need auditability and that logs don't leak. Also KMS—our keys stay in our HSM, so we need to understand how Redwood integrates.
[01:01] Maya: Got it. First off, how's your infra set up? Public cloud? single region?
[01:10] Leah: We're primarily on AWS. US-East and eu-west-1. Prod in US, EU for GDPR workloads. We currently have a NAT gateway for outbound, and an egress allowlist maintained in a WAF.
[01:25] Arjun: We also use a Transit Gateway for inter-VPC traffic. Some teams have VPC peering with partners. Our ask is: can Redwood present a stable set of egress IPs (or range) and support private endpoints inside our VPC?
[01:42] Diego: Short answer: yes for private endpoints and yes on stable egress IPs but depends on deployment model. For Redwood Private we can deploy in your VPC or we can set up private endpoints that terminate into our customer's VPC depending on the chosen topology. There's some nuance: when you host the dataplane in your VPC, egress IPs are your control; if we provide managed private endpoints from our infra, we'll provide fixed egress ranges per region.
[02:05] Samira: We prefer customer-hosted dataplane in our VPC, so keys never leave. Is that supported?
[02:12] Diego: Yes — Redwood Private offers a customer-managed dataplane package where inferencing runs on instances in your subnet and integrates with your KMS. You'd run the compute in your account. We'll need IAM role/workflows and some images.
[02:29] Leah: That sounds promising. But operationally we want minimal changes; we prefer peering to Transit Gateway if it's simpler. Any blockers to peering directly?
[02:40] Diego: VPC peering works well for north-south traffic if it's between two VPCs in same provider and accounts, but it doesn't support transitive routing. Because you have a Transit Gateway already, if you want multi-VPC connectivity across orgs, Transit Gateway might be cleaner at scale. For a single dedicated Redwood VPC <-> your VPC, peering is simplest.
[03:03] Arjun: What about DNS for private endpoints? We have private hosted zones.
[03:09] Diego: We recommend private endpoints backed by ENIs and mapping via Route53 private hosted zones. If you're running the dataplane in your VPC, you control DNS entirely. If using Redwood-managed private endpoints, we'll share DNS entries and you import or create a conditional forwarder. There's occasionally strange TTL stuff with some clients — we've seen resolvers that cache old entries.
[03:35] Tom: Ok, egress determinism—can you guarantee a single IP per region for outbound so our allowlist works?
[03:41] Maya: We can provide small ranges per account/region. If you need a single static IP, we'd recommend NAT in your account or using a static egress appliance in the VPC. Redwood-managed egress can give you fixed pools but not necessarily a single address unless you request a dedicated NAT instance.
[04:05] Samira: From compliance: we need audit logs for all inference requests and key usage. How are those surfaced?
[04:11] Diego: We provide audit logs at the control plane and request-level metadata. If you're self-hosting the dataplane, log collection can be forwarded to your logging endpoint (CloudWatch or ELK). Key usage logs remain in your KMS/HSM. We'll send example log schema.
[04:36] Leah: Latency tradeoffs — if we deploy compute in eu-west-1 for EU traffic, do we get lower latency? Any multi-region replication concerns?
[04:44] Diego: Yes, colocating inference in-region reduces RTT. We support multi-region model variants and can replicate model artifacts; replication adds storage and sync windows but it's automated. For strict residency you can pin traffic and model artifacts to a region.
[05:02] Arjun: A network detail — our security rule: we only accept peered ENIs with specific source prefixes and we do port 443 only. Are there additional ports for health checks or KMS calls?
[05:13] Diego: Primarily 443. For SSH or management you'll open ephemeral ports during onboarding; health probes are via TLS endpoints. KMS calls are outbound to AWS KMS endpoint in your region (443). If you use customer-hosted dataplane, inside your VPC calls to KMS don't exit.
[05:28] Samira: Okay. Another risky bit: we have a third-party data processor in GCP that needs to POST tokens to the inference endpoint — cross-cloud traffic. Any limitations?
[05:36] Maya: Cross-cloud is possible but depends on peering/handshake and egress policies. Often customers front endpoints with an internal API gateway that handles cross-cloud requests and enforces auth. We can support that pattern.
[05:51] Tom: On rollout: we'd start with a POC limited to a single model/route and a small traffic slice. How long to stand up a private dataplane in our VPC?
[05:58] Diego: With the prebuilt images and IaC templates it's a few days for engineers to provision, test, and validate — assuming you supply subnets, IAM role, and KMS access. If we manage the dataplane in Redwood infra, it's typically faster but less control.
[06:15] Leah: What's the SLA on Dedicated/Private? We need 99.9 for inference latency or at least predictable p95 figures.
[06:23] Maya: Dedicated capacity has SLOs and contractual SLAs; we can surface p50/p95/p99 from similar customers as reference. For private dataplane in your VPC, latency depends on instance sizing and your network. We'll help size and recommend GPU configs.
[06:37] Arjun: On the routing side — we operate egress filtering at Transit Gateway edge. If Redwood is peered to a single VPC we can NAT at that VPC's NAT and control egress. If you require Redwood-managed egress, we will want to confirm your firewall rules.
[06:53] Diego: Right — both are workable. For strict allowlist customers we often recommend the customer-run NAT appliance so they maintain the one-to-one mapping for IPs and can rotate as needed.
[07:07] Samira: KMS bit again — we use a third-party HSM with cross-account access. Do you support external key wrap (bring-your-own-key where Redwood never sees the plaintext)?
[07:16] Diego: We support envelope encryption and can configure the dataplane so the keys never leave your KMS. There's an onboarding step to exchange public keys and set IAM trusts. We'll need your security team's signoff.
[07:33] Leah: Could you sketch two topology options in the follow up: A) Redwood-managed private endpoints, B) Customer-hosted dataplane inside our VPC?
[07:40] Maya: Absolutely, Diego will prepare diagrams and call out port lists and routing implications.
[08:01] Tom: Any gotchas you've seen?
[08:03] Diego: A few: DNS caching oddities, unexpected MTU issues in cross-region peering, and forgotten STS role policies causing KMS failures. Also, some customers try to use very small NAT pools which saturate under bursty token generation.
[08:20] Arjun: We also worry about cost—if we run many instances in eu-west-1 what does autoscaling look like?
[08:27] Maya: Autoscaling policies are configurable; for private dataplane you control instance types. We can provide recommended scaling rules to keep cold start cost low and maintain p95 latency.
[08:42] Samira: On audit and compliance, can we get access to customer-specific audit streams?
[08:47] Diego: Yes — you can push logs to your CloudWatch/ELK. For control plane audit events we can ship JSON events to an S3 bucket with retention policies.
[09:05] Leah: Great. Let's talk timeline — we're targeting a Q2 pilot. How fast can Redwood provide a test account or a sandbox?
[09:12] Maya: We can spin up a sandbox in our EU region within a day for a limited test. For customer-managed dataplane it'll take provisioning time.
[09:20] Tom: Pricing note — for POC we'd like a trial of a few hundred thousand tokens and a short Dedicated window.
[09:26] Maya: We'll include trial credits and outline dedicated commit options in the follow up.
[09:33] (Side chatter)
[09:50] Diego: So recap — we'll send topology A/B, port lists, sample IAM policy, SOC2 and security docs, and a proposal for a pilot. We also want Arjun and Diego to do deep-dive next week.
[09:59] Leah: Sounds good.
[10:05] Maya: Anything else from team?
[10:10] Samira: One ask — sample timeline for SOC2 evidence collection if we onboard Redwood Private.
[10:16] Diego: We'll add that to the docs pack.
[10:35] Maya: Ok wrapping. Thanks all.

End transcript.

Notes: transcription has occasional speaker overlap and filler words. Some acronyms may be transcribed incorrectly (e.g., TGW vs. transit-gate).
